content:
The [Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator](/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Measure monthly debt commitments against gross income and see the income left after those payments. Enter your gross monthly income, monthly housing payment and other monthly debt payments and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Debt-to-income ratio (DTI) is the percentage of gross monthly income committed to recurring debt payments. Lenders use it as an affordability screen alongside credit history, employment stability, assets and living costs. This page separates housing expense from other obligations, calculates both common DTI views and shows what your listed commitments leave before tax, food, utilities and other everyday spending. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator

Start by entering your gross monthly income, then entering your monthly housing payment and finally entering your other monthly debt payments. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter monthly income before tax and payroll deductions.
2. Add rent or the full mortgage payment, including tax and insurance when those form part of the lender's housing figure.
3. Add minimum card, loan, lease, support and other required debt payments, excluding ordinary utilities and groceries.

## Formula

Total DTI = (monthly housing + other monthly debt payments) ÷ gross monthly income × 100. Housing DTI uses housing cost alone.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator](/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. With gross income of 6,500, housing of 1,600 and other debts of 550, total debts are 2,150. DTI is 2,150 ÷ 6,500 = 33.08%, and the housing-only ratio is 24.62%. Try the same figures in the [Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator](/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Gross monthly income: 6500, Monthly housing payment: 1600, Other monthly debt payments: 550), the [Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator](/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator) returns Total DTI: 33.1%, Housing-only ratio: 24.6%, Total monthly debt payments: 2,150, Income remaining after listed debts: 4,350, Debt payments at a 36% DTI: 2,340. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Loan Calculator](/loan-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Front-end and back-end DTI

Housing-only DTI is often called the front-end ratio. Total DTI, sometimes called the back-end ratio, includes housing plus other recurring debts. A 28% front-end and 36% back-end ratio is a familiar conservative guideline, not a universal approval rule. Some regulated mortgage programmes permit higher figures when other parts of an application are strong.

## A ratio is not a complete budget

DTI uses gross income and counts only selected obligations, so the percentage remaining is not disposable cash. Payroll tax, childcare, transport, food, insurance and savings can materially change affordability. Use this result as a lending benchmark and build a separate take-home-pay budget before committing to a new payment.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Use required minimum card payments rather than the full card balance.
- Do not include discretionary subscriptions or daily living costs as debt.
- Reducing a small recurring payment can help DTI more than a one-off purchase reduction.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a good debt-to-income ratio?

Lower is generally easier to manage. A total DTI at or below 36% is a common conservative benchmark, while lender and programme limits can be higher. Approval is never determined by DTI alone. Try it with your own numbers in the [Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator](/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Should I use gross or net income?

Lender DTI normally uses gross verified income. For personal budgeting, also calculate payments against take-home income because that better reflects available cash. Try it with your own numbers in the [Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator](/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Are utilities included in DTI?

Usually not. Standard DTI focuses on housing and reported recurring debt, although utilities still belong in your own affordability budget. Try it with your own numbers in the [Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator](/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator use?

Total DTI = (monthly housing + other monthly debt payments) ÷ gross monthly income × 100. Housing DTI uses housing cost alone. You can see it in action in the [Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator](/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
